# Plumbing scripts

A plumbing video solves one household problem cheaply, or settles one decision, for an older homeowner who would rather not pay for a service call. The winners in this niche (Got2Learn, Roger Wakefield, Silver Cymbal, TheCheapFix, and our own hits) get to the point fast, then give the viewer more reasons to stay by promising specific, priced payoffs, and pay those promises inside the video. This skill copies that shape for channels with no real person on camera.

## What this skill covers

**It owns:** the villain, the opening by video type, emotion all the way through, "point then promise", the structure of each video type and the list item shape, CTA placement, shape and length, length, voice, proof, money framing, safety and the plumbing scanner checks. Scripts are clean narration only: no edit notes, cues or directions of any kind.

**It doesn't own:**
- **The persona:** name, tenure, sign-off, any mentor or family detail. These live in the channel's persona profile.
- **The book and CTA wording:** also in the persona profile.
- **The claims policy, output format, voiceover copy and audit:** these live in the core rules.

**Authority:** the core claims policy and offer rules come first, then safety and the title's promise, then the persona profile, then this skill, then the core base rules. The core `workflow.md` runs every script (START, the input gate, the output format).

## Files in this skill

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `references/unit-plan-template.md` | The plan to fill in from the title and brief before any prose. |
| `references/price-guide.md` | Typical US prices for the jobs, parts and problems these channels talk about, each checked against at least two sources and re-checked by a second researcher. Used for any price the brief doesn't give. |
| `references/voice-samples.md` | Three stretches of real human narration from the real channels' winners: the voice anchor for every script (core `voice-anchoring.md`). |
| `references/excerpts.md` | Real lines grouped by job (the point, promises, money, limits, call-a-pro, comment questions). Lines from our hits and TheCheapFix are marked "structure only". Use for shape and range, never wording. |
| `references/models/INDEX.md` | The model library: 38 winning videos sorted by video type (two to nine per type; the never-do list has one, plus two list models for pacing). R files are real channels (structure and voice); S files are our hits and TheCheapFix (structure only). |
| `references/models/R01-...md` to `S18-...md` | One file per model: a beat map (what each stretch of the video does, with timings, items, promise devices, money and CTA placement; no wording), then the full labelled script, why it works and what doesn't transfer. Read at the planning step only. |
| `archive/` | Full transcripts of the four real channels. Calibration only; don't read them while writing. Kept in the library; the installed skill leaves it out, as the woodworking skill does. |

Every reference file, and this file itself, is under the copy guard: the scanner flags any run of 8 or more words shared with it (the files are listed in "Where this pack overrides the core", below). So the example lines in these rules show a shape; the script never reuses their wording.

## Inputs

Plumbing scripts are written from the title and the brief alone; there is no research pack. The workflow reads this block at START and won't write until every required input passes.

```inputs
- title | required | the locked title, exactly as approved
- brief | required | the ideation brief for this title; the script's facts, prices, doses and methods come from it first
- research-pack | not used | plumbing scripts are written from the brief
- rotation-log | required | the channel's last five ROTATION LOG ENTRY lines (from the earlier scripts in this chat, or pasted), or "none" for a new channel
```

- **The brief is the fact source,** with the price guide behind it. It does the research pack's job: the scanner checks every number in the script against the brief and `references/price-guide.md`, and the brief wins on safety.
- **No freshness check.** Prices are said as ranges (see "Money framing"), so nothing is re-checked at START.
- **Where the brief is silent, the script fills in** (P7, operator 2026-10-21):
  - **Prices** come from `references/price-guide.md`, said as an estimate: a rounded range or "about", never to the cent.
  - **The method, the right setting, how often to check, and what a mistake leads to** come from well-established, everyday plumbing knowledge, said plainly ("set the water heater to about 120 degrees", "test the shutoff once a year").
  - **No dose, mix or chemical method** beyond the brief and the five safe defaults in "Safety".
  - The run stops with NOT READY only when the brief can't carry the title's main promise, or a price the script needs is in neither the brief nor the price guide (then the cost is said in words instead, or the item is cut).

## The viewer

The viewer is a 50+ American homeowner, often in an older house and on a careful income, who would rather fix it than pay for a visit. They arrive from the feed, not from a search: they were offered a saving, a fear or a secret. Under the click sits one question: "Can I do this myself without making it worse?"

**What they bring, from the study's comments:**
- **The bill is the pain, not the plumber.** Comments name prices and labour often and the plumber rarely (8 of 506 on our hits). Many viewers like their own plumber, which is why the villain is aimed at the price.
- **They've already tried something.** The jug, the plunger, the fizzing volcano: "I tried an extra large size of Drano. That didn't work." A failed attempt is the strongest opening feeling in the data. Say why it failed in one plain sentence, then give the fix.
- **They have decades of habits.** "Never had a clog in 40 years." Confirm the good habits. When correcting a loved one (baking soda and vinegar), credit their thrift first: about 23 comments defended it against "it's theater."
- **They protect each other.** Safety corrections are among the most-liked comments (4.3K likes on borax not being boric acid). An unsafe line produces the angriest comments a channel gets.
- **They're impatient.** It's the commonest negative feeling in the study: "3:15 is where it starts." (2K likes). Get to the answer.
- **They ask the doing questions.** How much water, is it safe for septic, for plastic pipe, for old cast iron, which pipe do I have. Answer the ones that apply inside the script, at the step where they'd ask.
- **What they thank:** a fast answer, the reason why, a product they can find, steps clear enough to try, and the pride of doing it themselves ("72 years old and looking forward to seeing what else I can do").

**Skill level:**
- Write for beginners to handy homeowners, in plain words. A trade term gets a short explanation the first time ("the P-trap, the U-shaped bend under the sink"), then is used plainly.
- **These terms are always explained the first time** (test run 02 left five unexplained): psi, trap, P-trap, jetting, relining, anode rod, cleanout, PRV (pressure-reducing valve), angle stop, sillcock. Any other trade word gets the same treatment.
- Give the reason behind a step in one sentence; viewers thank the "why" (1.4K likes on Got2Learn). Don't lecture on the cause: "We don't need all that explanation of what causes the clog. Just tell us how to unclog it."
- Never explain what everyone knows (turning off a tap, fetching a bucket).

**The standard kit:**
- Assume the viewer owns a plunger, a bucket, old towels, rubber gloves, a flashlight, an adjustable wrench, pliers, a screwdriver, a measuring cup, and the usual kitchen and laundry products (baking soda, white vinegar, dish soap).
- Anything beyond that (drain snake, closet auger, wet-dry vac, pipe wrench, a specialty product) gets its typical price range and, where one exists, a cheaper alternative or an "optional."

For more depth, see `plumbing-ideation/references/audience.md` (§1 for this viewer, §4 for money language, §7 for safety).

---

## The villain

The villain on every plumbing channel is **the trade**: plumbers as a business, the plumbing industry, and whoever profits from the service call. Never a named company (core claims policy).

**How to use it, from what landed with viewers and what drew disbelief:**
- **Aim it at the price and the silence, not at motives.** "A drain call for that runs about $150" and "nobody in the trade will mention it" land. Claiming to know what plumbers secretly do at home, or that they hide fixes on purpose, drew the most-liked doubt in our data (1.3K likes).
- **Say it as a billing fact.** The trade is paid by the visit, so a $5 fix that ends the visits is nobody's business to mention. That's an observation the viewer can check against their own bills.
- **The villain comes back again and again, all the way through** (operator, 2026-10-21: "the villains need to be mentioned sporadically throughout"). One villain line in the opening, then every few items, not on a schedule and never in the same words twice: a price ("That's a $150 visit for a ten-minute job."), a silence ("Nobody's going to knock on your door and tell you about this one."), the store shelf, or the outrage line below.
- **Disgust at a big price, said as the narrator's opinion** (operator, 2026-10-21: "we must also show disgust to when things are very expensive"). Where a price runs into the hundreds or thousands, the narrator reacts as himself: "That is absolutely criminal, what they charge for that." Rotate the wording ("I think that's a crime for a part that costs less than lunch." "That number makes me sick."). It's aimed at the price, never at a named company, never at a person, and never says why they charge it (no "scam", no "ripping you off", no greed).
- **The store shelf is a second, softer villain:** the jug, the tablet, the marketing on the label. Use it where the fix replaces a product.

## The opening

Every opening, whatever the video type, does these jobs in about the first 45 seconds. Hooks are not one fixed formula: rotate the order and the shape across a channel's scripts (the rotation log tracks it), use the order for the video type (see "The video types"), or model the opening on one of the reference winner scripts for its shape and beats, never its wording. What can't change is that the point comes first and fast, and nothing on the banned list below appears.

1. **The point in the first sentence.** Name the title's subject and, wherever the title allows, the fix or product itself, by about 15 seconds. Never hold the name back: the two hits that hid the product for five and seven minutes drew the angriest comments in the study.
2. **A question, when it fits.** A question the viewer can answer in their own house ("When did you last lift the lid off your toilet tank?"), answered within about 15 seconds. Never a question the viewer can't check.
3. **The villain line,** as a price or a silence (above).
4. **Honest scope or reassurance,** in one line: what it won't do, or why it's safe ("It won't touch a hair clog." "Nothing here harms a septic tank."). This keeps the title's strongest word honest.
5. **The count line, when the video has a count** (a list, three fixes, eight checks; operator, 2026-10-25: "instead of saying 1 and 2 it would be better to say something like... the eight things you must check (if it doesnt already)"). One sentence naming the whole list and what it does for the viewer: "I'm going to show you the eight things you need to check before anybody quotes you a new tank." Skip it when the opening has already said the count. It never says what any single item holds: no "Number one is... Number two is...", no "Before we get to the fixes, you will hear...". Never "today" in front of it (the "today we're going to" ban below stands).
6. **The first real tip** by about 45 seconds; in a list, item one by about 30 seconds.

**Simpler and stronger** (operator, 2026-10-21: "it doesnt necessarily mean giving the worst case scenario. it means using strong words and targetting the exact pain points of this audience"). The first line hits the viewer's own pain in strong, plain words; it doesn't have to be the worst case.
- Before (test run 02): "That toilet pulled up off the floor, its drain packed solid with tree roots, didn't get that way overnight. A camera down the sewer line would've found those roots years earlier for a couple hundred bucks, and once they've taken over the line, you're into the thousands."
- The shape to aim for (never wording to reuse): "That slow flush you keep ignoring? It can end with a crew digging up your front yard. The expensive stuff in an old house always starts out quiet: a toilet that runs at night, a drip under the sink nobody sees, a rubber hose behind the washer that's older than you think. Fifteen of them, and almost every one takes a flashlight and five minutes to catch."
- **One dollar figure at most in the opening;** the prices belong to the items, and the opening never repeats item one's price.

**Never in an opening:** a name or channel intro, a greeting, "today we're going to", a recap of what's coming, a promise block or any run-down of what later items hold (operator, 2026-10-25), a first-person test or demonstration ("I tested", "watch me"), or a tenure number other than the profile's or the locked title's.

**Tenure:** at most once, as the profile's fixed number (Roger 45, Mark 40, Vintage 45) or, when the title states a different one, the title's number (title numbers win), and only where it does a job (credibility right before a verdict or a mistakes list).

## Emotion, all the way through

The operator (2026-10-21): "simpler and stronger on emotions... using strong words and targetting the exact pain points of this audience like reference scripts do. more work on emotion triggering throughout." Test run 02 named the pain once and then explained; the hits run on household pain plus money from the first line to the last: the bill, the thing that came back, the damage nobody saw, the bad night, the pride of doing it yourself. Every item makes the viewer feel something, in plain, strong words.

1. **Put the viewer in it.** Say "you" and open each item on what they see, hear or smell in their own house, not on how the thing works.
   - Did it: "You finish cooking up some bacon on a Saturday morning" (Roger, 453x hit).
   - Didn't: "Inside every tank water heater, a long metal rod hangs down from the top." (test run 02)
2. **Aim at one real pain per item,** the ones this audience lives with: the surprise bill; the fix that came back; damage you can't see; the bad night (water on the floor, no heat, the holiday rate); being sold something you didn't need; making it worse; the old house wearing out; the family's safety; the pride of doing it yourself.
3. **Strong, plain words.** Physical verbs and pictures over explanations: eating, rotting, packed solid, splitting, soaking, slime, sludge, "from the inside out", "while you sleep". Simple words, never clever metaphors (the Voice rule stands: at most one picture-phrase per item). Short sentences mostly, but two can and should sometimes be joined with "but" to keep the story flowing (operator, 2026-10-21).
4. **"But", much more of it, inside items and between them** (operator, 2026-10-21: "we want much more buts. both within sections and from section to section").
   - **Inside every item, at least one turn:** say what people think or do, then "but", then the truth. Did it: "most people think they are actually helping their pipes" (Roger, 453x hit). Test run 02 used "but" about once per 1,000 words; Silver Cymbal about 20.
   - **Between items, bridges that turn:** "But that one's cheap to fix. The next one isn't."
   - Rotate how the belief is named ("you've probably heard", "the box says", "a lot of folks figure"): "Most people…" opens a sentence at most once per script (`humanizer.md` H20), and a "but" turn is never the "it's not X, it's Y" reframe (H21, at most one).
5. **Ask the viewer.** A question they can answer about their own house, answered straight away, about every two items. Did it: "Problem solved, right? Not even close." (Roger, 453x hit). Test run 02 asked none.
6. **Use disgust where the topic has it.** Plumbing's unfair advantage, on the items about grease, gunk, hair, roots or what grows in a tank. Did it: "black, slimy, musty-smelling ring" (TheCheapFix). Test run 02 barely used it (0.3 disgust words per 1,000, against 2.4 in Roger's hit and 18.8 in TheCheapFix's).
7. **End every item on a win.** A short line of relief, pride or the contrast; the item's one price can sit here ("That's a $5 part doing a $300 visit's job."). Test run 02 ended 11 of 15 items on an instruction.
8. **Reaffirm the title's feeling all the way through** (operator, 2026-10-21: "we must reaffirm throughout the emotions we are trying to trigger from the title and concept"). Come back to the title's idea and its key word, one way or another, every few items: for "15 Plumbing Mistakes Quietly Costing You THOUSANDS", the mistake and the hidden, growing bill ("another mistake that costs you while you sleep", "quietly", "adding up"). Not on every item, and never so often it turns robotic or repetitive (operator, after test run 03: "in one way or another it should be referred to more than it was. not every item though"). Test run 02 never said "mistake" or "quietly" after the opening; test run 03 said "mistake" only in its first line.
9. **The villain and the outrage come back** all the way through (see "The villain").
10. **Let the narrator speak.** One short "I" opinion or verdict in most items ("I'd leave that jug on the shelf"), and once per video a line of insistence where it matters ("I need you to hear me on this one"). Test run 02 had no verdict from item 10 to 15.
11. **Finish on relief, not danger.** The last item before the end CTA closes on reassurance or something to do tonight, even when it's a safety item.

**Never, still:** invented facts or events, guaranteed savings, the trade's motives, teases, the mocked hype ("horror movie", "brutal tests"), worst-case exaggeration, jokes.

## Point then promise

The competitors give the point first and promise second; our hits did the reverse and made the viewer wait. From now on:

- **Point first.** The first answer (the fix named, the rule stated, the first verdict fact) comes before anything else.
- **Pay forward lines fast.** A later item named in a forward line is paid within about five minutes. Nothing is promised in the opening (operator, 2026-10-25).
- **Keep one promise open.** After the opening, never go more than about five minutes without a new forward line or a payoff. Use a line that names the next value ("The next one is the reason your tank sweats in July."), the trade's price for what was just done, a question the next item answers, or a check the viewer can run.
- **Every callback has a promise.** A line that says "I promised" or "like I said" must match something the script really promised earlier.
- **A priority flag at the first answer,** in fresh words each time (the shape: "If you do only one thing from this video, do this one."). Viewers pointed at that line when it came late.
- **No recaps** at the end.

## Ways to promise more value

Use two or three per video, in the body only (never as a list in the opening), and rotate them across a channel's scripts.

- **A numbered item with its money stake:** "Number four can save you a $300 camera inspection."
- **A numbered item with its stake in words:** "Number eight is the step that protects old cast-iron pipe."
- **The escalation ladder:** the cheap fix, then the stronger fix, then the point to call, with the trade's typical price as the top rung. The default for fix videos.
- **The rule that protects everything:** a safety or method rule, named at the first item it touches, paid straight after the first fix or as the last item.
- **A second use for the same product,** or "while you're under there".
- **A check the viewer can run:** lift the lid, the food-colouring test, the fizz test. No first-person test claim needed.
- **A running cost tally** across the video (what the trade would have charged so far).
- **The trade's price at the end of each item** (in words on the items without a figure: the number cap in "Money framing").
- **A problem the viewer didn't know they had,** promised and then shown.
- **A myth flag,** which names the belief it flips in the same line: "Number three is the one everybody gets backwards: hot water and dish soap won't carry grease away." Never a bare "the one everybody gets backwards".

## The video types

Pick the type from the title. Each type has its own opening order and item shape. These are the most common types, not the only ones (operator, 2026-10-21). The models column names example files in `references/models/` (R = real channels, structure and voice; S = our hits and TheCheapFix, structure only); `references/models/INDEX.md` lists every model for each type. Never copy their wording, and follow "Using the models" below.

| Type | Title shape | Opening, in order | First tip by | Item shape | Models |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Single-product fix** | "1 Cup of This…", "Pour X Into Y Tonight" | Product and what it does → reassurance → the doubt answered ("Too simple? It works on…") → what the jug or the visit costs → what it won't do | 40-60 s | Dose, method, wait time, what you'll see, when it won't work | R07, R15, R19, R20; S06, S08, S14, S15 |
| **N things about one product** | "N Things Plumbers Don't Want You to Know About X" | The product in the viewer's house and its price → what the trade charges for the same jobs → "nobody will mention it" → the belief it flips → the count line | 45-90 s | A scene, what the trade charges, the method with amounts, the payoff | S01, S05, S17, S18; R02 and R10 for list pacing |
| **Never-do list** | "N Things You Should NEVER…" | A habit doing hidden damage → the avoidable cost → the trade bills for the result → the count line | 30-45 s | The habit, why it does damage, what to do instead | S03; R16 for list pacing |
| **Mistakes list** | "N Mistakes That…", "DO NOT Install X Until…" | A symptom question or neglect → the cost in hundreds or thousands → one credibility line → the count line | 15-30 s | The mistake, what it costs, the right way | S04, S16; R09 |
| **Head-to-head verdict** | "X vs Y vs Z: A [tenure]-Year Plumber's Verdict" | The failed attempt or the moment of choice → the contenders with prices → everyone disagrees, the pitch sells the dear one → "each one gets a job" → one concrete extra | 45-60 s | Each contender: what it's for, what it's not for, one line of verdict; then which to use for which job | R04; S02, S11, S12 |
| **Banned / code explainer** | "Here's Why X Is NOT ALLOWED Anymore" | The why-question, or the viewer finding the fixture → the rule, scoped ("most codes", never "illegal") → the reason and one real danger, in proportion → "if yours works, you may not need to change it" → the fixes | about 20 s | Rule, reason, verdict, the fixes from cheapest | R01; S10 |
| **How-to / correct way** | "The CORRECT Way to X", "How to X (Before It…)" | The task and the number-one mistake, or the myth flipped → "you can do this" → the step count line → when not to do it | 15-45 s | One step, the reason, the mistake to avoid | R03, R08, R13, R14; S09 |
| **Product swap** | "X Is Expensive. Use THIS Instead!" | The pro's price → the usual DIY option and its catch → the popular shortcut, judged fairly → the swap named, with its price and where not to use it | about 60 s | The swap, the price, the job it fits | R05, R18 |
| **Hidden cause** | "Why Your X Keeps Y" | The thing the viewer trusts → what it's really doing → the hidden cause in one line → "what that means for you", answered at once | 30-45 s | Cause, how to check, the fix | R06, R17; S07 |
| **Seasonal or emergency** | "Do This Before the First Freeze" | The clock and the crisis → "put the phone down" with the after-hours price → "probably nothing's broken" → the cause in one line → the fixes with what the viewer already owns | 30-45 s | The step, why now, what to watch for | R11, R12, R17; S13 |

A title that promises tests ("I Tested 5 Drain Cleaners") is written as tests and results from the brief, never as "I tested".

### The item shape in lists

The hits give every item the same order, so viewers can follow it and retell it (the top comment on Roger's 453x hit, 1.5K likes, is a viewer listing all five). In every list type (N things, never-do, mistakes), each item runs in this order; the table's item shape says what goes into it.

1. the scene in the viewer's house
2. what's really happening in the pipe (one or two lines)
3. what it costs, once (a figure or in words; see "Money framing")
4. the turn ("So what do you do instead?")
5. the fix, with its steps cut to what the viewer needs
6. the win

- **Length per item:** about 100-130 words (45 seconds to a minute) in a list of 10 or more is the guide, and an item may run a bit longer as long as nothing in it is fluff (operator, after test run 03, whose items ran about 140-200 words: "fine if it runs a bit longer. as long as its not fluff"). Cut extra steps, repeated warnings and restated points first; test run 02's long items were mostly extra steps. Where the guide and the 12-minute minimum collide (a list of 10 or 11 items), the minimum wins, again with real value, never padding.
- **Bridges:** never more than two items in a row without a forward line or a price line. Test run 02 went from item 7 to item 12 without one.

**A title that fits none of the ten:** build the opening from the six jobs in "The opening", in the order the closest type uses, and pick the item shape from the table that best suits the content. Note the title in the plan as "new type". When the same new shape comes up on three or more videos, it's proposed for this table, and added only with the operator's yes.

## Using the models: never a copy

The models show how winning videos are built. A script borrows their structure, never their wording, and never one model's structure whole.

1. **Name the models and the differences.** The plan names the model or models used and at least three things done differently: the opening order, the number or order of items, the promise devices, the money device, or the comment question.
2. **No repeats.** The same model is never used twice in the channel's last five scripts. This pack adds fields to the core rotation log entry, `| model: [file numbers]` among them (see "Where this pack overrides the core").
3. **Blending is encouraged:** the opening shape from one model and the item pacing from another, for example.
4. **Planning only.** Model files are read at the planning step, never kept open while writing. Wording comes fresh from the brief, in the persona's voice.
5. **The audit checks it:** the plan lists its differences, and no model in it appears in the last five rotation log lines.

The copy guard still flags any run of 8 or more words shared with a model file.

A model's promise block is never copied: several of our hits and TheCheapFix's open with one, and this pack no longer does (operator, 2026-10-25). The excerpts' group 5 lines are for forward lines in the body.

## CTAs

- **Roger the Pipe Guy and Mark Silverbridge:** back to the structure their hits used (HANDOFF, locked 2026-10-20). Roger's hits used the same shape in three videos (7:14 in the 364x hit, about 37% of the way in). Only the order transfers: its opening words ("if you're finding this…") are a banned stock line.
  - **Where:** about a third of the way in, never before the end of item 3 (in a list of 15, after item 4 or 5), at the end of an item's win, never in the middle of a forward line. Test run 03 put it after item 3, at 23%; the operator: "push it out a bit later".
  - **The shape, in about 60-80 words:**
    1. an aside signal ("By the way", "Quick thing", "Before the next one", rotated)
    2. tied to the help just given ("if that one just saved you a service call")
    3. this is a small part of it: the book has the rest, with the pages from the book match when the topic's in the book
    4. one benefit
    5. where to get it: the link in the description and the QR code
    6. a return line into the next item
  - **An example of the shape (never wording to reuse):** "Quick thing before number four. If that toilet check just saved you a service call, that's one of a hundred fixes in my book, One Hundred Old-House Fixes That Save You Thousands. The sewer warning signs from number one are on pages 56 and 57. It's at the link in the description, or use the QR code on your screen. Now, the hose on your outside faucet."
  - **At the end,** a one-line reminder, then the comment line (see "The ending"). Wording comes from the persona profile.
- **The Vintage Pipefitter:** no mid-video CTA. At the end, a one-line subscribe ask, worded in the persona profile. Something fuller (an email CTA) will be decided later.
- **Never a long QR walkthrough,** never the same pitch twice in one video, and never a production label read aloud.

## The ending

Every plumbing channel ends the way Bertha's Clean Home does: the video's last line is a real attempt to get a comment. This overrides core `cta-and-endings.md` §4 for plumbing (P5).

After the last item:
1. **The end CTA: a one-line reminder,** in the persona profile's words, on every channel.
2. **The comment ask, which ends the video:** a short turn from the book line to the viewer so it doesn't land abruptly, an outright ask to leave a comment ("in the comments", "leave me a comment"), one specific question the viewer can answer from their own house plus one small detail about them, and "I read every one." Two or three sentences. The shape (never wording to reuse): "Before you go, I want to hear from you. Down in the comments, tell me how old your house is and which drain gives you the most grief. I read every one." Never a bare "let me know in the comments" without the question, and never the same question two videos running. (Test run 03 went straight from the book line to "Tell me…" without ever saying to comment; the operator: "didnt actually say to comment. it was too abrupt".)

There's no fixed last line or sign-off after the comment ask. No recap, no tease of a future video, and nothing after the comment line.

## Length

**At least 12 minutes** of narration on every plumbing script (this pack raises the core 8-minute minimum): 1,800 spoken words at 150 a minute, or at the profile's words per minute. **12 to 20 minutes is the sweet spot.** Inside that, the value decides: words per item depend on the item.

- **Never pad to reach a length.** Cut repetition instead: the same check said twice five minutes apart, or the promise restated, is padding.
- **If the brief can't fill 12 minutes with real value,** even with the fill-ins above, the run stops with NOT READY and asks for a fuller brief (more items, more detail). The fix belongs at the ideation stage, not in extra words.
- **For calibration, not as targets:** our hits ran 17 to 21 minutes, and the competitors' median was about 13. The length complaints on our hits were about the wait before the answer and the repetition, not the runtime: TheCheapFix and Arrow ran as long and drew about one length complaint each.

## Voice

Our hits sounded more like a person than our recent uploads: 1.5-2 times the first person on all three channels, more "you", and plain routine lines where the recent uploads used crafted metaphor. Even the hits used the least first person of any human-voiced channel in the study (5.3-8.8 per 1,000 words against 15.2-25.1).

- **"You" for every instruction; "I" for opinions, preferences and verdicts.** "Pour it in slowly." "I'd leave the jug on the shelf for old cast iron." Write in contractions, the way people talk, unless the persona profile forbids them (Mark Silverbridge's does: no contractions anywhere).
- **Plain beats clever.** State the fact. At most one picture-phrase per item, and only when it teaches ("a colony of bacteria wearing a glue coat" explains biofilm). Mark's similes rose from 0.3 to 1.7 per 1,000 words in his recent uploads, with nothing to show for it.
- **Honest candor.** Say the limits plainly: "Peroxide does not dissolve rock." "Nothing in plumbing is permanent." These are the lines viewers call honest. Never an invented mishap.
- **Warmth comes from reassurance, not humour.** "You're fine." "Nothing's broken." "There's no shame in calling a pro." No jokes (a portfolio-wide decision).
- **Swearing: none** in plumbing scripts. (The woodworking allowance doesn't carry over; nothing in the plumbing study calls for it.)
- **A persona device only if the profile has one:** a mentor line or a household routine (Roger's first-Saturday check; Mark and Vintage have none). At most twice per video, under about 40 words, to teach or warn, never as proof that something works. Its facts (names, ages, places) come from the profile and never change.
- **A phrase is voice once; in the same slot every video, it's a tic.** Vintage used "Nine times out of 10" in 9 of 10 videos. Each stock phrase at most once per video, and rotate what opens an item and what closes the video. (The list of limited phrases comes with "Banned in these scripts".)

## Proof

The clearest difference in the study: the face channels, and Got2Learn filming his own hands, drew no complaints about the footage, while our hits drew about 38 (Mark about 28). Most of that is the camera. But the script made it worse every time it said "I tested", "watch me" or "look at". Proof in these scripts is the kind that survives any footage.

**Use:**
- **The mechanism, in one plain line:** why it works. "Its entire job is to corrode so your tank does not." The best ones are under 15 words.
- **A number from the brief or the price guide, said as a typical range** rather than one exact price: "somewhere between $400 and $800 for the unit." Sources and store names don't have to be said, and a source is named only rarely, where it really helps ("the Department of Energy puts it at…"). **When the script names a source, its figure is said as the source gives it** (the price guide's $36 to $61, not $35 to $60); without the name, round as usual (operator, after test run 03).
- **The maker's own warning,** when the brief confirms one: "Kohler, American Standard and Toto all warn against chlorine tablets in their own instructions."
- **A check the viewer runs at home,** with what they'll see either way: the fizz test for old peroxide, food colouring in the tank for a leaking flapper. Only checks the brief confirms really work (food colouring can't find a leak at the toilet's base).
- **The honest limit:** what the fix won't do. "Peroxide does not dissolve rock."
- **Exact amounts, waits and what "done" looks like:** "One cup of washing soda stirred into two or three cups of hot tap water. Leave it six to eight hours." Check the arithmetic of every dose: one hit called two cups "half of a 16-ounce bottle" (it's the whole bottle), and four comments caught it.
- **The typical case, as a general statement:** "Plenty of people replace a toilet when the rim jets only needed cleaning."

**Never:**
- **First-person tests, trials or demonstrations,** even when the title promises tests. "I put all three through eight brutal tests" drew "Where is the footage of him doing the tests?" Tests and results are fine when the brief gives them, said without "I": "In pull tests, the push-fit gave way first." "Side by side, the enzyme cleaner took three nights; the jug took fifteen minutes and the clog was back in a week."
- **Anything that needs footage the channel doesn't control:** "watch me", "look at the toilet on the left", "there's a stack of receipts on my bench right now".
- **Customer stories and results:** "I had a homeowner tell me…", "an exterminator quoted a lady three hundred dollars". The claims policy bans customers; say it as the typical case instead.
- **Nameless claimed experience:** "the worst tank we've ever opened".
- **Sweeping claims nobody can check:** "this trick has saved homeowners across America hundreds of dollars".

## Money framing

All 15 of our hits set the fix's cost against what the trade charges. In this niche that comparison is the entry ticket, not an extra. The weak spot is a single low product price: viewers check it on Amazon while they watch. Service-call ranges drew almost no disputes.

**1. The comparison comes early,** within the first two minutes, usually as the villain line.
- Did it: "That little brown bottle sitting in your medicine cabinet cost about $1 at most drug stores. And yet the average homeowner pays a plumber $300 or more every single year…" (TheCheapFix, 2.18M views; first sentence).
- Didn't: Vintage's enzyme video names no product and no price at the point; the per-night cost arrives more than five minutes later.

**2. Every price is an estimate, from the brief or the price guide:** a rounded range or "about", never one exact figure and never to the cent. Not every item needs a number. A list with a dollar figure on every item is too much to follow on one listen (the Hank tests, 2026-10-20; test run 02 said 25 dollar amounts on 11 of 15 items).
- **The number cap** (operator, 2026-10-21): at most one dollar figure per item (a range counts as one); in a list, figures on no more than about half the items, and the rest carry their cost in words ("that's a new water heater", "a flooded basement", "a service call"); the opening has one figure at most and never repeats item one's. The brief decides what things cost; this rule decides how many numbers are said.
- The money devices below all work inside the cap: on items without a figure, the trade's price is said in words ("that's a visit you didn't pay for").
- Drew fire: "usually around eight to twelve dollars a bottle" brought "This guy prices are from 1924, Amazon - BIO-CLEAN $79.95." "A dollar or two" for peroxide brought "Peroxide is now priced close to 5.00 since COVID." TheCheapFix's "$1 a bottle" brought "Maybe 30 years ago!" (48 likes).
- Survived: "An after hours no heat call lands somewhere between $200 and $400 in most of the country, more at night or on a weekend" (Mark). No disputes.
- Write: "A flapper runs about $5 to $15. Having someone fit it usually starts around $150."
- **How to say a range** (operator, 2026-10-21): give the spread and why it moves, or the top of it.
  - "This can cost you anywhere from $200 to $400, depending on where you live and how bad it's got."
  - "On the high end, this can run up to $20,000."
  - Rotate these shapes and the reason given (where you live, the size of the job, the age of the house, a weekend call); never the same phrasing twice in one video.

**3. The cost per use, when a product lasts,** checked against the dose.
- Did it: "That box is about $4 to $5 and it gives you the better part of a dozen treatments. Call it 50 cents a pop." (Roger, hit).
- Check: "a box lasts two years of monthly treatments" has to survive the arithmetic. A 55-ounce box at half a cup a month doesn't make two years.

**4. Rotate the money devices** across a channel's scripts, so no two videos count money the same way:
- **Three prices side by side:** "50 cents versus 20 bucks versus 300. That's the whole game." (Roger, hit).
- **The trade's price at the end of each item:** "This is exactly what professional kitchen cleaning services charge $40 a visit for. You just did it for cents." (TheCheapFix, hit).
- **A running total,** closed at the last item: "Total spent, $2. Total saved off the new toilet, right around 500." (Vintage, hit).
- **Payback arithmetic for big purchases** (water heaters, softeners, tankless): "If you save $20 a month, but spend an extra three, four grand to install it, it's going to take you over 12 years just to break even." (Roger Wakefield, hit).

**5. Say it when the cheap or popular option loses.** "That is a 30-year payback period. That is not great." (Mark, his biggest hit). A verdict that says no is the one viewers trust, and "the one situation where paying somebody is the cheap option" (Mark) keeps the villain honest.

**6. A money figure in the title is paid at its item,** with what was avoided spelled out. TheCheapFix's "#4 Saves $300" lands at item four as the new toilet nobody has to buy: "you absolutely do not need to pay a plumber $300 to $500 to replace your fixture."

**7. Brand names are optional.** Name a widely sold product only when it is the answer and the brief confirms it's on sale now. Viewers acted on the one brand our hits named: "I ordered some Arm & Hammer super washing soda… The water is draining for the first time in months!" (304 likes).

**Never:**
- **A guaranteed saving** (claims policy). Not "this saves you $300", but "this can save you the $300 visit".
- **The trade's motives** (see "The villain"). Not "that's how he pays his mortgage", but "a drain call starts around $150".
- **A total stated as certain** when it depends on the viewer's house. Not "this is a $5 fix", but "if it's the flapper, that's a $5 to $15 fix".

## Safety

The facts and methods come from the brief, and **the brief always wins**. There's no separate fact bank: contradictions between one video and another are acceptable.

**Defaults, only where the brief is silent.** These five drew the angriest comments in the study (about 18 on boiling water and 17 on washing soda that set hard: "Thanks to this video I had to hire a plumber!"), so the script uses the safe version unless the brief says otherwise:
1. **Hot tap water,** not boiling water, for drains, toilets and plastic pipe.
2. **Washing soda dissolved first** in hot tap water, not poured in dry.
3. **One cleaner at a time;** never bleach with ammonia, vinegar or any acid, or peroxide with vinegar. Peroxide means the 3 percent drugstore bottle.
4. **Nothing added to a drain that already has a chemical drain cleaner in it,** plunging included. It can splash back.
5. **Gas lines and live wiring are a call, not a project.** Before any water-heater job, the power or the gas goes off, in one line.

**A gas leak, whenever a script mentions one, gets every step** in the gas-leak row of `references/price-guide.md` section 9, whatever the brief leaves out, in the script's own words. The steps, in short: everyone out, upwind; no switches, appliances, doorbells, phones or flashlights; no flame, no car; 911 and the gas company from well away, never assuming someone else called; back in only when they say so; they turn the gas on and relight; not everyone can smell it, and the smell fades. Never "open the windows" or "shut it off at the meter yourself". (Test run 02 left out "don't light anything or start a car".)

**How safety sounds:**
- **One short line inside the step where the risk is,** with the reason, in proportion. "It will put you on the floor" (chlorine gas) drew no complaints; vague danger drew "This is nothing but a scare tactic video."
- **The call-a-pro line names its trigger:** "Two drains backing up at once is the main line. That's a call." Never the vague "if it's outside your comfort zone", and never a long list of stop signs.

## Banned in these scripts

**Never:**
- **A name or channel intro,** a greeting, "today we're going to", or "this channel is for…" (all three channels used the same channel-promise line in their recent uploads).
- **Vague teases:** "stay till the end", "stick with me", "by the end of this video" and the rest of the core hard-ban list. Concrete, named promises are the plumbing exception (P3), in the body only.
- **A recap** at the end.
- **First-person tests and demonstrations:** "I tested", "I tried", "my results", "watch me".
- **Pointing at the screen:** "look at the one on the left", "as you can see", "right here", "look at this".
- **Customer stories and results, the trade's motives,** and anything negative stated as fact about a named company.
- **Edit notes, cues, labels or directions** of any kind.
- **The recent template's stock lines,** which showed no lift and made the three channels sound alike: "not a scam, just economics" (and "no conspiracy", "just arithmetic"); "this channel is for / exists / is all about"; "grab it now or later"; "your wallet (or pipes) will thank you"; "they just don't volunteer it"; "if you're finding this helpful"; "let's continue"; "common problems you might run into".
- **Hype that got mocked:** "horror movie", "brutal tests", and any "every" or "forever" the script then walks back.
- **Competitors' catchphrases and sign-offs.**
- **Copying 8 or more words in a row** from a reference file. The copy guard flags it.

**At most once per video.** A phrase is voice once; in the same slot every video it's a tic. "Nine times out of 10" is fine, and it's on this list with the others: "between you and me", "ask me how I know", "here's the part nobody tells you", "I'll be straight with you", "that's the whole trick", "in your pocket", "which brings us", "hold that thought", "the big one", "the real kicker", "quick thing", "no shame in", "full stop", "trust me", "absolutely criminal".

## Scanner rules for this niche

The scanner (core `script-scanner.py`) reads this block. `allow` lines are wording these rules require (the range shapes, the comment line's close), so the copy guard over this file never flags them; `ban` lines are fix-on-sight; `once` lines fail on the second use in a script (scanner support built 2026-10-21, test 20). There are no checks for boiling water or dry washing soda: the brief wins on safety, and the operator said "dont even flag them" (2026-10-21).

```scanner
min-minutes: 12
allow: on the high end
allow: depending on where you live
allow: I read every one
ban-regex: \btoday,? (?:we'?re|we are|I'?m|I am) going to\b | opening: "today we're going to"
ban-regex: \bI(?:'ve| have)? (?:tested|tried|ran (?:a |the |some |my )?tests?)\b | first-person test claim
ban-regex: \bmy (?:own )?(?:test|tests|testing|results)\b | first-person test claim
ban: watch me | first-person demonstration
ban: as you can see | pointing at the screen
ban-regex: \blook at the \w+(?: \w+)? on the (?:left|right)\b | pointing at the screen
ban-regex: \bnot a scam\b|\bisn'?t the scam\b|\bjust (?:plain )?(?:economics|arithmetic)\b|\bno conspiracy\b | template stock line: the economics aside
ban-regex: \bthis channel (?:is for|exists|is all about)\b | template stock line: channel promise
ban: grab it now or later | template stock line
ban-regex: \byour (?:wallet|pipes) will thank you\b | template stock line
ban-regex: \b(?:just )?(?:do not|don'?t) volunteer it\b | template stock line
ban-regex: \bif (?:you'?re|you are) finding this helpful\b|\bif this is helping\b | template stock line
ban-regex: \blet'?s (?:continue|keep going)\b | template stock line
ban: common problems you might run into | template stock line
ban: horror movie | hype that got mocked
ban-regex: \bbrutal tests?\b | hype that got mocked
once-regex: \bnine (?:times )?out of (?:10|ten)\b | nine times out of 10
once: between you and me
once: ask me how I know
once-regex: \bhere(?:'?s| is) the part (?:people skip|nobody tells you)\b | here's the part nobody tells you
once-regex: \bI(?:'?ll| will) be (?:straight|square|honest) with you\b | I'll be straight with you
once-regex: \bthat(?:'?s| is) the whole (?:trick|method|job|game)\b | that's the whole trick
once: in your pocket
once-regex: \bwhich (?:brings us|leaves)\b | which brings us
once-regex: \bhold that thought\b|\bput a pin in\b | hold that thought
once: the big one
once: the real kicker
once-regex: \bquick (?:thing|pause|one)\b | quick thing
once: no shame in
once: full stop
once: trust me
once: absolutely criminal
```

## Before handing over

Check that:
- the point comes in the first sentence, with the fix or product named by about 15 seconds, and the first line hits the viewer's pain in strong, plain words
- every item puts the viewer in the scene, aims at one real pain, has at least one "but" turn and ends on a win; bridges turn between items; a question about every two items; the title's feeling comes back every few items; the villain comes back all the way through, with disgust at the big prices as an opinion (never a company or a motive); the last item before the end CTA closes on relief
- in a list, every item follows the item shape at about 100-130 words (lists of 10 or more; a bit longer is fine, fluff never is), and no more than two items in a row go without a forward line or a price line
- the opening follows the video type's order (or the closest type's, for a new type), with no intro, greeting, tease or recap
- no promise block: the opening names no single later item and ends on the count line (when there's a count) or item one; every forward line is paid within about five minutes, and no stretch runs past about five minutes without a forward line or a payoff
- the tenure appears at most once, as the profile's number or the title's
- every price traces to the brief or the price guide and is said as an estimate (never cents, at most one per item, figures on no more than about half the items, one at most in the opening); doses and waits trace to the brief or the safe defaults; filled-in settings and intervals are everyday knowledge; the dose arithmetic holds
- the fix's cost meets the trade's price within the first two minutes
- there's no "I tested", no pointing at the screen, no customer story and no motive
- safety follows the brief, with the five defaults only where it's silent; a gas leak gets every step from the price guide; every trade term on the list is explained the first time; a myth flag names its belief
- the CTAs follow the persona profile: the mid-video ask about a third of the way in, never before the end of item 3, in the six-part shape (Roger and Mark), and a one-line end CTA on every channel (Roger and Mark: the book reminder; Vintage: the subscribe ask)
- the video ends on the comment ask (a turn to the viewer, an outright ask to comment, a specific question and "I read every one"), with nothing after it
- each stock phrase appears at most once, and the opening shape and money device differ from the rotation log
- the plan names its models with at least three differences, and no model was used in the channel's last five scripts
- the script runs at least 12 minutes (12 to 20 is the sweet spot), with nothing padded
